They were worshippers of idols like the polytheists of Makkah, so Allah warned Quraysh that a punishment would befall them that would uproot them if they did not believe. Nuh (peace be upon him) was the first prophet sent, and he is called the Shaykh of the Messengers and the Second Adam. He is Nuh son of Lamak, son of Matushalakh, son of Khanukh, who is Idris son of Bard, son of Mahalayil, son of Anush, son of Qaynan, son of Shith, son of Adam, peace and blessings be upon them.

﴿That warn your people﴾: it is permissible that "an" (أنْ) be a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, and that it be an explanatory (tafsiriyyah) particle.

﴿A painful punishment﴾: Ibn Abbas said: the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. Al-Kalbi said: what befell them of the flood.

﴿Of your sins﴾: "min" (مِن) is for partitive (lil-tab'id), because faith only erases what preceded it of sins, not what comes after. It was said: it is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah). It was said: it is extra (za'idah), and this is the view of Ibn Atiyyah, who said: the Kufan school. I say: it is the view of al-Akhfash, not of the Kufans, because they stipulate that after "min" there must be an indefinite noun, and they do not mind what precedes it of obligatory or other. Al-Akhfash permits it with the obligatory and otherwise. It was said: it applies to both the indefinite and the definite. It was said: it is for clarifying the genus, and this was rejected on the grounds that there is nothing before it that it clarifies.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how did He say 'and give you respite' while He has informed that the term cannot be deferred? Is this not a contradiction?" I say: Allah decreed, for example, that if the people of Nuh believed, He would give them a life of a thousand years, and if they remained upon their disbelief, He would destroy them at the end of nine hundred years. So it was said to them: believe, and He will give you respite until a specified term, that is, until a time that Allah named and set as a limit that you reach and do not exceed, which is the longer time, the completion of the thousand. Then He informed that when that appointed limit comes, it is not deferred as this time is deferred, and you will have no stratagem, so hasten during the times of reprieve and delay. End of quote. Ibn Atiyyah said: "And He will give you respite until a specified term" is among what the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites) relied upon in their saying that a person has two terms. They said: if it were one fixed term, deferral would not be valid, if the limit had already arrived, nor hastening if it had not arrived. He said: they have no basis in the verse, because the meaning is that Nuh (peace be upon him) did not know whether they were among those who would be deferred or among those who would be hastened, and he did not say to them that you will be deferred beyond a term that has already come upon you. Rather, it had already been decided in eternity that they were either among those for whom faith and deferral were decreed, or among those for whom disbelief and hastening were decreed. Then this meaning was reinforced and made clear by His saying: "Indeed, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not deferred." The answer to "if" (لَوْ) is omitted; its estimate is: "if only you knew," you would have hastened to worship Him, fear Him, and obey me in what I brought you from Him, exalted is He. When they did not respond to him and harmed him, he complained to his Lord with the complaint of one who knows that Allah, exalted is He, is Knowing of his situation with his people, since he was commanded to warn and did not find (faith) among them.

﴿He said: "My Lord, indeed I have called my people night and day"﴾: that is, at all times, without slackness or neglect at any time. When they increased in turning away and aversion from the truth, the calling became what increased them, since it was the cause of increase. Similar to it is: ﴿So it increased them in filth upon their filth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125].

﴿Indeed, every time I called them so that You might forgive them﴾: that is, so that they would repent and You would forgive them. He mentioned the cause, which is their own pure benefit, so that their aversion from it would be more ugly. ﴿They put their fingers in their ears﴾: the apparent meaning is literal: they blocked their hearing so that they would not hear what he called them to, and they covered themselves with their garments so that they would not look at him, out of aversion and hatred of hearing the advice and seeing the advisor. It is also permissible that it be a metaphor for the extreme of their turning away from what he called them to; they were like one who blocks his hearing and prevents his sight. Then he repeated the description of his calling for clarification and emphasis. When he mentioned the generality of times in his calling, he mentioned the generality of states of calling. And "every time I called them" indicates the repetition of calls (p-339), without specifying the state of his first call. Its apparent meaning is that his calling was in private, because that is gentler to them, and perhaps they would accept from him, like one who advises in secret, for such a person is likely to be accepted. When he did not find success in private, he moved to something stronger, which is calling them openly, clearly, to Allah without sparing anyone. When that did not work, he returned to proclamation and to private speech.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of "then" (ثُمَّ) is to indicate the distance between states, because openness is more severe than privacy, and combining the two is more severe than singling out one of them. End of quote. Al-Zamakhshari often repeated that "then" is for indicating remoteness, and we do not know this from the words of anyone else. "Openly" (جِهارًا) is in the accusative by "I called them," and it is one of the two kinds of calling. There is in it the same disagreement found in the accusative of "he walks swaying" (al-khawzala). Al-Zamakhshari said: or because he intended by "I called them" their open gathering. It is permissible that it be a description of the verbal noun of "called" meaning "a call openly," that is, announced publicly; or a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial state, that is, publicly declaring.

Then He informed that He commanded them to seek forgiveness, and that if they sought forgiveness, provision would flow to them in this world. He put first what would delight them and what is more beloved to them, since the soul is eager to obtain what is immediate, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And another you love: help from Allah and a near victory﴾ [al-Saff: 13]; and: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed and feared Allah, We would have removed from them their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Bliss. And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66], the verse; and: ﴿And that if they had remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. Qatadah said: they were people who loved the world, so He called them to the Hereafter by the path they loved. It was said: when they denied him after a long repetition of the calling, they suffered drought and their women became barren, so He began in His promise with rain, then followed it with wealth and children.

"Abundant" (مِدْرارًا): from "flowing abundantly" (الدَّرّ), and it is an adjective in which the masculine and feminine are equal; "mif'al" does not take the feminine "ta'" except rarely, so the masculine and feminine share it. You say: a man who is mihdamah and mitrabah, and a woman who is mihdabah and mitrabah. And "the sky" (السَّماءُ) is that which is above. It was said: because rain descends from it to the clouds. It is also permissible that "the sky" means the clouds and the rain, as in the line of verse:

"When the sky descends upon the land of a people"... the verse.

"Hope" (الرَّجاءُ) has two meanings: fear and hope. Abu Ubaydah and others said: ﴿You do not hope﴾ means "you do not fear." They said: "dignity" (الوَقارُ) means greatness and authority. The statement according to this is a threat and a warning. It was said: "you do not hope for Him to be revered," that is, you do not expect for Him reverence. Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is: what is the matter with you that you are not in a state in which Allah's greatness toward you would be in the abode of reward? "For Allah" is an explanation of the one who is revered; had it been placed later, it would have been a complement. Or: "you do not fear Allah's forbearance and His refraining from hastening punishment upon you, so that you would believe." It was said: what is the matter with you that you do not fear Allah's greatness. From Ibn Abbas: "You do not fear for Allah an outcome," because the outcome is the state of the settling of affairs and the firmness of reward and punishment, from "waqara" meaning "he became firm and settled." End of quote. It was said: what is the matter with you that you do not make your hope in Allah and before Him a dignity, and it would be according to this that they are as if saying: a deliberation from you and a steadiness in consideration, because thought is the place of lightness, recklessness, and headstrong behavior. End of quote. In al-Tahrir, Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "What is the matter with you that you do not hope for Allah for reward, nor fear His punishment," and Ibn Jubayr said this from Ibn Abbas. al-Awfi said from him: "What is the matter with you that you do not know Allah's greatness." From Mujahid and al-Dahhak: "What is the matter with you that you do not care for Allah's greatness." Qutrub said: this is a Hijazi dialect, and Hudhayl, Khuza'ah and Mudar say: "lam arju" (I did not hope), "lam ubali" (I did not care).

﴿You do not hope﴾: a circumstantial state (hal). ﴿While He has created you in stages﴾: a circumstantial clause, which is to be understood as a call to faith in Allah and to singling Him out in worship, since in this circumstantial clause there is an alert to the gradual progression of the human through stages that could only come from His creation, exalted is He. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid said: from the drop, the clinging clot, and the lump of flesh. It was said: in the difference of people's colors, forms, characters, and religions. It was said: children, then youths, then elders, then weak and then strong. It was said: the meaning of "stages" (atwar) is: kinds, healthy and sick, seeing and blind, rich and poor.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 71, verses 15–28 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: (p-340) ﴿Have you not seen how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon in them a light, and made the sun a lamp?﴾ ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth.﴾ ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a [definite] bringing forth.﴾ ﴿And God has made the earth for you a spread-out carpet.﴾ ﴿That you may travel therein along roads, wide ways.﴾ ﴿Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him not except in loss.﴾ ﴿And they have plotted a great plot.﴾ ﴿And they have said, 'Do not leave your gods, and do not leave Wadd or Suwa' or Yaghuth and Ya'uq and Nasr.'﴾ ﴿And they have already misled many. So increase not the wrongdoers except in error."﴾ ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter the Fire, and they found for themselves, besides God, no helpers.﴾ ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant.﴾ ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and not beget except wicked, ungrateful disbelievers.﴾ ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house believing and the believing men and believing women. And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction."﴾

When Noah, peace be upon him, alerted them to reflect upon themselves, and how they passed from one state to another, and the self is the nearest thing about which they reflect, he directed them to reflect upon the world, its upper and lower parts, and what God, exalted is He, placed in it. That is, in the upper world, of these two luminaries by which the existence of the universe is sustained. The explanation of (ṭibāqan, "in layers") has already been given in Surat al-Mulk. The pronoun in (fīhinna, "in them") refers to the heavens. It is said that the moon is in the lowest heaven. It is correct that the heavens be a container (ẓarf) for the moon, because it does not necessarily follow from a container that the contained fills it. You say, "Zayd is in the city," and he is in a part of it. The sun is not restricted to a container, so it is said: it is in the fourth, and it is said: in the fifth, and it is said: in winter it is in the fourth, and in summer in the seventh. This is something whose knowledge cannot be attained except from the science of astronomy (ʿilm al-hay'a). The people of this science mention that conclusive proofs stand for them confirming what they claim, and that in knowing that there is clear evidence of the greatness of God, His power, and the wondrous nature of His creation.

(Sirājan, "a lamp") by which the people of the world are illuminated, just as people are illuminated by a lamp in their houses. The moon did not reach the degree of the sun in brightness; therefore He said: "He who made the sun a radiance (ḍiyā') and the moon a light (nūr)," and ḍiyā' is stronger than nūr.

The (inbāt, "causing to grow") is a metaphor for creation. He created Adam from the earth, and his offspring came from him; therefore it is correct to attribute all of them to having been caused to grow from it. The accusative of (nabātan, "a growth") governed by (anbatakum, "caused you to grow") is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the extra element omitted, meaning a causing to grow; or it is by an implied verb, meaning: "so you grew a growth." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "He caused you to grow, so you grew," or it is in the accusative by (anbatakum) because it includes the meaning of (nabatum, "you grew"). End. I do not understand the meaning of this second opinion that he mentioned.

(Then He will return you into it) meaning: He will make you buried in it. (And bring you forth in a bringing forth) meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, and He emphasized it with the verbal noun, meaning: that is certainly going to happen.

(Carpet) you turn over upon it as a man turns over on his carpet. Its apparent meaning is that the earth is not spherical, but spread out. (Subulan, "roads") means ways; (fijājan, "wide") means broad. The discussion of (al-fajj, "wide path") has already passed in Surat (p-341) al-Ḥajj.

When they persisted in disobedience and treated him with the worst of words and deeds, (Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me"). The pronoun is for all of them. He had said to them: "And obey me," and he had remained among them the length God Most High specified: "a thousand years less fifty years" [al-ʿAnkabut: 14]. They had been given such abundance of provision that they would harvest twice in a month. (And followed) means: their common people and lowest, since it is not correct for the pronoun to return to all of them in the worship of idols.

(Whom wealth and children increase not) means: their leaders and great ones, those whose accumulated wealth and whose multitude of children were a cause of their loss in the Hereafter, and were the cause of their destruction in this world. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-A'raj, Mujahid, the two brothers (al-Akhawan, i.e., Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi', in the transmission of Kharija, read (wulduhu, "his children") with a ḍamma on the waw and sukūn on the lam. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan also, Abu Raja', Ibn Thabbat, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with fatḥa on both, and they are two dialects, like (bukhlun and bukhulun, "stinginess"). Al-Hasan also, al-Jahdari, Qatada, Zirr, Talha, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu ʿAmr, in one transmission, read it with kasra on the waw and sukūn on the lam. Abu Hatim said: it is possible that (al-wuld, with ḍamma) is the plural of (al-walad, "child"), like (khashab and khushub, "wood"). Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"O Bakr of Amina, blessed is her firstborn, of the sons of a chaste woman, with the fortunate Sa'd."

(And they plotted): it appears that it is conjoined to the relative clause of (man, "whom"), and the pronoun in (wa-makarū, "and they plotted") and (wa-qālū, "and they said") is plural by sense. Their plotting was their scheming in religion and inciting people against Noah, peace be upon him. The majority read (kubbāran, "great") with shadda on the bāʾ, and it is a form that has much intensification. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: it is a Yemeni dialect, and upon it is the saying of the poet:

"A man is attached to the youths of generosity by the character of the noble, and not by beauty (wuḍḍāʾ)."

And the saying of another:

"A white woman who hunts hearts and captivates with beauty the heart of the Muslim reciter."

It is said: ḥussān, ṭuwwāl, and jummāl (intensive forms). ʿIsa, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu al-Sammal read it with the bāʾ lightened, and it is an intensive form. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn Muḥaysin, as narrated from him by Abu al-Ukhayrit Wahb ibn Wadih, read (kibbāran) with a kasra on the kāf and fatḥa on the bāʾ. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a plural of (kabīr, "great"), as if he made "plotting" in place of "sins" or "deeds," and this is the end; he means that for this reason it was described with the plural.

(And they said), that is, their great ones to their followers; or they said, that is, all of them, some to others: (Do not abandon, "lā tadharunna" meaning: do not leave) (your gods), that is, your idols; this is general for all their idols, and then certain ones were specified after the chief idols, namely Wadd and what is conjoined to it. It is narrated that these were names of righteous men who lived in the early times. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: they were children of Adam, and Wadd was the greatest of them and the most devoted to him. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Muhammad ibn Qays said: they were sons of Adam and Noah, peace be upon them both; when they died, their forms were fashioned so as to remind people of their righteous deeds; then those who had fashioned them died, and others succeeded them who venerated them, and so on until they were worshipped. It was said: then those idols were transferred in their very forms. And it was said: rather only the names were transferred, to tribes of the Arabs. So Wadd belonged to Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal; Suwa' to Hudhayl, and it is said: to Hamdan; Yaghuth to Murad, and it is said: to Madhhij; Ya'uq to Hamdan, and it is said: to Murad; and Nasr to Himyar, and it is said: to Dhu al-Kala' of Himyar. For this reason the Arabs named people ʿAbd Wadd and ʿAbd Yaghuth. What occurred of this disagreement concerning Suwa', Yaghuth and Ya'uq may be that each of them had an idol named by this name, since it is far-fetched that the actual idols should survive; rather only the names remained, and they named their idols by them. Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi said: I saw Yaghuth, and it was of lead, carried upon a bare-backed camel; they travelled with it and did not provoke it until it was the one that knelt, and when it knelt they dismounted and said: "It has approved the resting place for you," so they would dismount around it and pitch a structure for it. End. Al-Tha'labi said: Yaghuth belonged to Kahlan of Saba', passed down among them until it came to Hamdan, and in it Malik ibn Namat al-Hamdani says:

(p-342) "God makes feathers in the world and cuts them, but Yaghuth neither cuts nor makes feathers."

Al-Mawardi said: Wadd is the name of a worshipped idol; it was named Wadd because of their affection for it (widd). End. It was said: Wadd was in the form of a man, Suwa' in the form of a woman, Yaghuth in the form of a lion, Ya'uq in the form of a horse, and Nasr in the form of a vulture; and this contradicts what preceded, that they fashioned the forms of righteous people. Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Shayba, with a difference from them, read (wuddan) with ḍamma on the waw; al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, Talha, and the rest of the seven read it with fatḥa. The poet said:

"May Wadd greet you, for we do not find it lawful for us the amusement of women, and the religion has decided."

Another said:

"So may Wadd greet you, from your love I met [her], and the gazelles upon the high ground of Tulala, sleeping."

It was said: he meant that idol. The majority read (wa-lā yaghūtha wa-yaʿūqa, "nor Yaghuth and Ya'uq") without tanwin. If they are Arabic, then their non-declension is due to definiteness and the form of the verb; if they are foreign, then due to foreignness and definiteness. Al-Ashhab read (yaghūthan wa-yaʿūqan) with tanwin on both. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: he made them a form (fa'ūl), and therefore he declined them. As for the common reading, they are two adjectives derived from (al-ghawth, "help") and (al-ʿawq, "hindrance") as verbs, and they are definite, so they are not declined, because two verbal features are combined: definiteness and resemblance to the imperfect verb. End. But this is confused. First, they cannot be a form (fa'ūl), because the root of yaghuththu is missing, and likewise ya'uqqu. Second, they are not adjectives derived from (al-ghawth) and (al-ʿawq), because (yafʿal) does not come as a noun or adjective; they were prevented from declension only for the reason we mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: al-Aʿmash read (wa-lā yaghūthan wa-yaʿūqan) with declension, and that is an error, because definiteness is binding and the verb pattern. End. But this is not an error; al-Aʿmash did not stand alone in this, rather al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli agreed with him. Its explanation is in one of two ways. The first: it came in the dialect of those who decline all that is not declined in the common Arabic usage, and this is a dialect, which al-Kisa'i and others narrated. The second: it was declined for the sake of matching what precedes and follows it of the indefinite, since before it is (wuddan wa-lā suwā'an, "Wadd nor Suwa'") and after it (wa-nasran, "and Nasr"), as they said regarding the declension of (salāsila, "chains") and (qawārīra qawārīra, "crystal, crystal") for whoever declines them for the sake of matching. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a problematic reading, because if they are Arabic or foreign there is non-declension in them; perhaps he intended the matching of endings, so he declined them because they correspond to their sisters which are declined: (wuddan wa-suwā'an wa-nasran), just as it was read (wa-ḍuḥāhā, "and its morning") with imāla because it occurs together with the imāla-forms for the sake of matching. End. Al-Zamakhshari did not realize that there is a dialect of some Arabs that declines everything that is not declined in the common usage, and therefore he found it problematic.

(And they have already misled) means: the leaders who are followed, (many): of their followers and common people. This is Noah, peace be upon him, informing about them of the misguidance that happened at their hands. Al-Hasan said: (and they have misled) means: the idols, the pronoun returning to them as it returns to rational beings, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "My Lord, they have indeed led astray many of the people" [Ibrahim: 36]; and it is made better by its return to the nearest mentioned referent, but its return to the leaders is more apparent, since they are the ones spoken of, and the meaning is more applicable to them. When he informed that they had gone astray much, he prayed against them for misguidance, saying: (And do not increase). It is conjoined to (and they have misled), since its implied sense is: "He said, and they have misled many"; so it is governed by the implied (said), whose quoted speech is (and they have misled). Harmony is not a condition in conjoining sentences; rather one may conjoin a sentence of command upon a sentence of information and the reverse, contrary to those who claim harmony is required. Al-Zamakhshari said, summarized: he conjoined (and do not increase) upon (My Lord, they have disobeyed me), meaning he said these two statements.

(Except in error). Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): how is it permissible that he should want error for them and call upon God to increase it? (I say): what is meant by error is that they be forsaken and deprived of divine favors, because of their obstinacy in disbelief and the despair of their belief; and that is good and beautiful, and it is permissible to supplicate with it, rather it would not be good to supplicate with the opposite. End. This is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. He said: it is also possible that error means ruin and perdition, as He said: "And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction." Ibn Bahr said: (except in error) means: except in punishment, as in His saying: "Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness" [al-Qamar: 47]. It was said: except in loss. It was said: except in error concerning the affairs of their worldly life and the furthering of their plots and stratagems.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 71, verses 15–28 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of readers recited ﴿مِمّا خَطِيئاتِهِمْ﴾ (mimma khatee'atihim, "because of their sins") as a plural with the alif and ta', with hamza. Abu Raja' also recited it this way, except that he replaced the hamza with a ya' and assimilated the madd ya' into it. Al-Jahdari and Ubayd, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, recited it in the singular, with hamza. Al-Hasan, 'Isa and al-A'raj are reported to have recited it in more than one way. Abu 'Amr read khataya-hum as a broken plural (jam' taksir). This is a statement from Allah, Exalted, to the Messenger (ﷺ) that the supplication of Nuh (peace be upon him) has been answered. The ma here is extra, for emphasis (za'ida li-l-tawkid). As for (min), Ibn 'Atiyya said it indicates the starting point of the action (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), but it appears that it indicates causation (li-l-sabab).

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited: min khatee'atihim ma ughriqu, with ma inserted between ughriqu and khatee'atihim. The majority recited (ughriqu) with hamza. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited ghurriqu with the shaddah. Both forms mean transitive causation (li-l-naql). Their sins (khatee'at) are shirk and what follows from it of the major sins. ﴿فَأُدْخِلُوا نارًا﴾ ("so they were made to enter a fire"): that is, Jahannam. The future is expressed in the past tense to indicate its certainty, and it is joined with fa' to indicate the intended sense of a ruling. Or the entry is used to express their being exposed to the Fire morning and evening, as He says: ﴿النّارُ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("The Fire, they are exposed to it," Ghafir: 46). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or what is meant is the punishment of the grave." End of quote. Al-Dahhak said: they were drowned from one side and burned with fire from another side.

﴿فَلَمْ يَجِدُوا لَهم مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أنْصارًا﴾ ("and they did not find for themselves, besides Allah, any helpers"): an allusion to the absence of the power of their gods to help them. The supplication of Nuh (peace be upon him), after it had been revealed to him that ﴿لَنْ يُؤْمِنَ مِن قَوْمِكَ إلّا مَن قَدْ آمَنَ﴾ ("None of your people will believe except those who have already believed," Hud: 36), was said by Qatadah. Also from him: he did not invoke against them except after Allah had brought forth every believer from the loins, and had rendered the wombs of their women barren. This does not appear correct, because he said: ﴿إنَّكَ إنْ تَذَرْهم يُضِلُّوا عِبادَكَ﴾ ("If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants," and so on), and his saying ﴿ولا يَلِدُوا إلّا فاجِرًا كَفّارًا﴾ ("and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers") indicates that he had not rendered their wombs barren. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd also said this, but it does not appear to be as we have said, and he had previously been hopeful of their faith and compassionate towards them. In a hadith: "Some of them would strike him at times until he fell unconscious; when he recovered he would say: 'O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"

(Dayyaran): this is among the words of generality which are used in negation and similar contexts. Its pattern is fayyal, its root is diwar; the ya' and the waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so they were assimilated. It is said that from it comes dawwar, whose pattern is fa''al; both come from al-dawaran (circling), just as they say qiyam and qiwam, and the meaning is the meaning of ahad. From al-Suddi: one who dwells in a house. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is fayyal from al-dawr or from al-dar. End of quote. Al-dar is also from al-dawr, and its alif is converted from a waw.

﴿ولا يَلِدُوا إلّا فاجِرًا كَفّارًا﴾ ("and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers"): he described them, in the state of their begetting, by what they would come to of wickedness and disbelief. When he invoked against the disbelievers, he asked forgiveness for the believers, beginning with himself, then with those whose goodness was obligatory upon him, then for the believing men and women; so it is as though he and his parents were included among the believing men and believing women. The majority recited (wa-li-walidayya) ("and for my parents"), and it is apparent that the two of them are his father Lamak ibn Matushalakh and his mother Shamkha' bint Anush. It was also said: they are Adam and Hawwa'. Ibn Jubayr and al-Jahdari recited (wa-li-walidi) with a kasra on the dal, so either he specified his nearest father, or he meant all those who begot him back to Adam (peace be upon him). Ibn 'Abbas said: no father of Nuh (peace be upon him) between him and Adam (peace be upon him) disbelieved. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri and Zayd ibn 'Ali recited (wa-li-waladaya), the dual of walad, meaning Sam and Ham.

﴿ولِمَن دَخَلَ بَيْتِيَ﴾ ("and for whoever enters my house"): Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: my mosque. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: my law (shari'ati); he borrowed the word "house" for it, just as they say "the dome of Islam" and its "tent." It was also said: his ship. It was said: his dwelling.

﴿ولِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ والمُؤْمِناتِ﴾ ("and for the believing men and believing women"): he invoked for every believing man and woman in every nation. Al-tabar means destruction.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 71, verses 15–28 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: (p-340) ﴿Have you not seen how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon in them a light, and made the sun a lamp?﴾ ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth.﴾ ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a [definite] bringing forth.﴾ ﴿And God has made the earth for you a spread-out carpet.﴾ ﴿That you may travel therein along roads, wide ways.﴾ ﴿Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him not except in loss.﴾ ﴿And they have plotted a great plot.﴾ ﴿And they have said, 'Do not leave your gods, and do not leave Wadd or Suwa' or Yaghuth and Ya'uq and Nasr.'﴾ ﴿And they have already misled many. So increase not the wrongdoers except in error."﴾ ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter the Fire, and they found for themselves, besides God, no helpers.﴾ ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant.﴾ ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and not beget except wicked, ungrateful disbelievers.﴾ ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house believing and the believing men and believing women. And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction."﴾

When Noah, peace be upon him, alerted them to reflect upon themselves, and how they passed from one state to another, and the self is the nearest thing about which they reflect, he directed them to reflect upon the world, its upper and lower parts, and what God, exalted is He, placed in it. That is, in the upper world, of these two luminaries by which the existence of the universe is sustained. The explanation of (ṭibāqan, "in layers") has already been given in Surat al-Mulk. The pronoun in (fīhinna, "in them") refers to the heavens. It is said that the moon is in the lowest heaven. It is correct that the heavens be a container (ẓarf) for the moon, because it does not necessarily follow from a container that the contained fills it. You say, "Zayd is in the city," and he is in a part of it. The sun is not restricted to a container, so it is said: it is in the fourth, and it is said: in the fifth, and it is said: in winter it is in the fourth, and in summer in the seventh. This is something whose knowledge cannot be attained except from the science of astronomy (ʿilm al-hay'a). The people of this science mention that conclusive proofs stand for them confirming what they claim, and that in knowing that there is clear evidence of the greatness of God, His power, and the wondrous nature of His creation.

(Sirājan, "a lamp") by which the people of the world are illuminated, just as people are illuminated by a lamp in their houses. The moon did not reach the degree of the sun in brightness; therefore He said: "He who made the sun a radiance (ḍiyā') and the moon a light (nūr)," and ḍiyā' is stronger than nūr.

The (inbāt, "causing to grow") is a metaphor for creation. He created Adam from the earth, and his offspring came from him; therefore it is correct to attribute all of them to having been caused to grow from it. The accusative of (nabātan, "a growth") governed by (anbatakum, "caused you to grow") is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the extra element omitted, meaning a causing to grow; or it is by an implied verb, meaning: "so you grew a growth." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "He caused you to grow, so you grew," or it is in the accusative by (anbatakum) because it includes the meaning of (nabatum, "you grew"). End. I do not understand the meaning of this second opinion that he mentioned.

(Then He will return you into it) meaning: He will make you buried in it. (And bring you forth in a bringing forth) meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, and He emphasized it with the verbal noun, meaning: that is certainly going to happen.

(Carpet) you turn over upon it as a man turns over on his carpet. Its apparent meaning is that the earth is not spherical, but spread out. (Subulan, "roads") means ways; (fijājan, "wide") means broad. The discussion of (al-fajj, "wide path") has already passed in Surat (p-341) al-Ḥajj.

When they persisted in disobedience and treated him with the worst of words and deeds, (Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me"). The pronoun is for all of them. He had said to them: "And obey me," and he had remained among them the length God Most High specified: "a thousand years less fifty years" [al-ʿAnkabut: 14]. They had been given such abundance of provision that they would harvest twice in a month. (And followed) means: their common people and lowest, since it is not correct for the pronoun to return to all of them in the worship of idols.

(Whom wealth and children increase not) means: their leaders and great ones, those whose accumulated wealth and whose multitude of children were a cause of their loss in the Hereafter, and were the cause of their destruction in this world. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-A'raj, Mujahid, the two brothers (al-Akhawan, i.e., Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi', in the transmission of Kharija, read (wulduhu, "his children") with a ḍamma on the waw and sukūn on the lam. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan also, Abu Raja', Ibn Thabbat, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with fatḥa on both, and they are two dialects, like (bukhlun and bukhulun, "stinginess"). Al-Hasan also, al-Jahdari, Qatada, Zirr, Talha, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu ʿAmr, in one transmission, read it with kasra on the waw and sukūn on the lam. Abu Hatim said: it is possible that (al-wuld, with ḍamma) is the plural of (al-walad, "child"), like (khashab and khushub, "wood"). Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"O Bakr of Amina, blessed is her firstborn, of the sons of a chaste woman, with the fortunate Sa'd."

(And they plotted): it appears that it is conjoined to the relative clause of (man, "whom"), and the pronoun in (wa-makarū, "and they plotted") and (wa-qālū, "and they said") is plural by sense. Their plotting was their scheming in religion and inciting people against Noah, peace be upon him. The majority read (kubbāran, "great") with shadda on the bāʾ, and it is a form that has much intensification. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: it is a Yemeni dialect, and upon it is the saying of the poet:

"A man is attached to the youths of generosity by the character of the noble, and not by beauty (wuḍḍāʾ)."

And the saying of another:

"A white woman who hunts hearts and captivates with beauty the heart of the Muslim reciter."

It is said: ḥussān, ṭuwwāl, and jummāl (intensive forms). ʿIsa, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu al-Sammal read it with the bāʾ lightened, and it is an intensive form. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn Muḥaysin, as narrated from him by Abu al-Ukhayrit Wahb ibn Wadih, read (kibbāran) with a kasra on the kāf and fatḥa on the bāʾ. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a plural of (kabīr, "great"), as if he made "plotting" in place of "sins" or "deeds," and this is the end; he means that for this reason it was described with the plural.

(And they said), that is, their great ones to their followers; or they said, that is, all of them, some to others: (Do not abandon, "lā tadharunna" meaning: do not leave) (your gods), that is, your idols; this is general for all their idols, and then certain ones were specified after the chief idols, namely Wadd and what is conjoined to it. It is narrated that these were names of righteous men who lived in the early times. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: they were children of Adam, and Wadd was the greatest of them and the most devoted to him. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Muhammad ibn Qays said: they were sons of Adam and Noah, peace be upon them both; when they died, their forms were fashioned so as to remind people of their righteous deeds; then those who had fashioned them died, and others succeeded them who venerated them, and so on until they were worshipped. It was said: then those idols were transferred in their very forms. And it was said: rather only the names were transferred, to tribes of the Arabs. So Wadd belonged to Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal; Suwa' to Hudhayl, and it is said: to Hamdan; Yaghuth to Murad, and it is said: to Madhhij; Ya'uq to Hamdan, and it is said: to Murad; and Nasr to Himyar, and it is said: to Dhu al-Kala' of Himyar. For this reason the Arabs named people ʿAbd Wadd and ʿAbd Yaghuth. What occurred of this disagreement concerning Suwa', Yaghuth and Ya'uq may be that each of them had an idol named by this name, since it is far-fetched that the actual idols should survive; rather only the names remained, and they named their idols by them. Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi said: I saw Yaghuth, and it was of lead, carried upon a bare-backed camel; they travelled with it and did not provoke it until it was the one that knelt, and when it knelt they dismounted and said: "It has approved the resting place for you," so they would dismount around it and pitch a structure for it. End. Al-Tha'labi said: Yaghuth belonged to Kahlan of Saba', passed down among them until it came to Hamdan, and in it Malik ibn Namat al-Hamdani says:

(p-342) "God makes feathers in the world and cuts them, but Yaghuth neither cuts nor makes feathers."

Al-Mawardi said: Wadd is the name of a worshipped idol; it was named Wadd because of their affection for it (widd). End. It was said: Wadd was in the form of a man, Suwa' in the form of a woman, Yaghuth in the form of a lion, Ya'uq in the form of a horse, and Nasr in the form of a vulture; and this contradicts what preceded, that they fashioned the forms of righteous people. Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Shayba, with a difference from them, read (wuddan) with ḍamma on the waw; al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, Talha, and the rest of the seven read it with fatḥa. The poet said:

"May Wadd greet you, for we do not find it lawful for us the amusement of women, and the religion has decided."

Another said:

"So may Wadd greet you, from your love I met [her], and the gazelles upon the high ground of Tulala, sleeping."

It was said: he meant that idol. The majority read (wa-lā yaghūtha wa-yaʿūqa, "nor Yaghuth and Ya'uq") without tanwin. If they are Arabic, then their non-declension is due to definiteness and the form of the verb; if they are foreign, then due to foreignness and definiteness. Al-Ashhab read (yaghūthan wa-yaʿūqan) with tanwin on both. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: he made them a form (fa'ūl), and therefore he declined them. As for the common reading, they are two adjectives derived from (al-ghawth, "help") and (al-ʿawq, "hindrance") as verbs, and they are definite, so they are not declined, because two verbal features are combined: definiteness and resemblance to the imperfect verb. End. But this is confused. First, they cannot be a form (fa'ūl), because the root of yaghuththu is missing, and likewise ya'uqqu. Second, they are not adjectives derived from (al-ghawth) and (al-ʿawq), because (yafʿal) does not come as a noun or adjective; they were prevented from declension only for the reason we mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: al-Aʿmash read (wa-lā yaghūthan wa-yaʿūqan) with declension, and that is an error, because definiteness is binding and the verb pattern. End. But this is not an error; al-Aʿmash did not stand alone in this, rather al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli agreed with him. Its explanation is in one of two ways. The first: it came in the dialect of those who decline all that is not declined in the common Arabic usage, and this is a dialect, which al-Kisa'i and others narrated. The second: it was declined for the sake of matching what precedes and follows it of the indefinite, since before it is (wuddan wa-lā suwā'an, "Wadd nor Suwa'") and after it (wa-nasran, "and Nasr"), as they said regarding the declension of (salāsila, "chains") and (qawārīra qawārīra, "crystal, crystal") for whoever declines them for the sake of matching. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a problematic reading, because if they are Arabic or foreign there is non-declension in them; perhaps he intended the matching of endings, so he declined them because they correspond to their sisters which are declined: (wuddan wa-suwā'an wa-nasran), just as it was read (wa-ḍuḥāhā, "and its morning") with imāla because it occurs together with the imāla-forms for the sake of matching. End. Al-Zamakhshari did not realize that there is a dialect of some Arabs that declines everything that is not declined in the common usage, and therefore he found it problematic.

(And they have already misled) means: the leaders who are followed, (many): of their followers and common people. This is Noah, peace be upon him, informing about them of the misguidance that happened at their hands. Al-Hasan said: (and they have misled) means: the idols, the pronoun returning to them as it returns to rational beings, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "My Lord, they have indeed led astray many of the people" [Ibrahim: 36]; and it is made better by its return to the nearest mentioned referent, but its return to the leaders is more apparent, since they are the ones spoken of, and the meaning is more applicable to them. When he informed that they had gone astray much, he prayed against them for misguidance, saying: (And do not increase). It is conjoined to (and they have misled), since its implied sense is: "He said, and they have misled many"; so it is governed by the implied (said), whose quoted speech is (and they have misled). Harmony is not a condition in conjoining sentences; rather one may conjoin a sentence of command upon a sentence of information and the reverse, contrary to those who claim harmony is required. Al-Zamakhshari said, summarized: he conjoined (and do not increase) upon (My Lord, they have disobeyed me), meaning he said these two statements.

(Except in error). Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): how is it permissible that he should want error for them and call upon God to increase it? (I say): what is meant by error is that they be forsaken and deprived of divine favors, because of their obstinacy in disbelief and the despair of their belief; and that is good and beautiful, and it is permissible to supplicate with it, rather it would not be good to supplicate with the opposite. End. This is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. He said: it is also possible that error means ruin and perdition, as He said: "And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction." Ibn Bahr said: (except in error) means: except in punishment, as in His saying: "Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness" [al-Qamar: 47]. It was said: except in loss. It was said: except in error concerning the affairs of their worldly life and the furthering of their plots and stratagems.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 71, verses 15–28 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of readers recited ﴿مِمّا خَطِيئاتِهِمْ﴾ (mimma khatee'atihim, "because of their sins") as a plural with the alif and ta', with hamza. Abu Raja' also recited it this way, except that he replaced the hamza with a ya' and assimilated the madd ya' into it. Al-Jahdari and Ubayd, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, recited it in the singular, with hamza. Al-Hasan, 'Isa and al-A'raj are reported to have recited it in more than one way. Abu 'Amr read khataya-hum as a broken plural (jam' taksir). This is a statement from Allah, Exalted, to the Messenger (ﷺ) that the supplication of Nuh (peace be upon him) has been answered. The ma here is extra, for emphasis (za'ida li-l-tawkid). As for (min), Ibn 'Atiyya said it indicates the starting point of the action (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), but it appears that it indicates causation (li-l-sabab).

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited: min khatee'atihim ma ughriqu, with ma inserted between ughriqu and khatee'atihim. The majority recited (ughriqu) with hamza. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited ghurriqu with the shaddah. Both forms mean transitive causation (li-l-naql). Their sins (khatee'at) are shirk and what follows from it of the major sins. ﴿فَأُدْخِلُوا نارًا﴾ ("so they were made to enter a fire"): that is, Jahannam. The future is expressed in the past tense to indicate its certainty, and it is joined with fa' to indicate the intended sense of a ruling. Or the entry is used to express their being exposed to the Fire morning and evening, as He says: ﴿النّارُ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("The Fire, they are exposed to it," Ghafir: 46). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or what is meant is the punishment of the grave." End of quote. Al-Dahhak said: they were drowned from one side and burned with fire from another side.

﴿فَلَمْ يَجِدُوا لَهم مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أنْصارًا﴾ ("and they did not find for themselves, besides Allah, any helpers"): an allusion to the absence of the power of their gods to help them. The supplication of Nuh (peace be upon him), after it had been revealed to him that ﴿لَنْ يُؤْمِنَ مِن قَوْمِكَ إلّا مَن قَدْ آمَنَ﴾ ("None of your people will believe except those who have already believed," Hud: 36), was said by Qatadah. Also from him: he did not invoke against them except after Allah had brought forth every believer from the loins, and had rendered the wombs of their women barren. This does not appear correct, because he said: ﴿إنَّكَ إنْ تَذَرْهم يُضِلُّوا عِبادَكَ﴾ ("If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants," and so on), and his saying ﴿ولا يَلِدُوا إلّا فاجِرًا كَفّارًا﴾ ("and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers") indicates that he had not rendered their wombs barren. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd also said this, but it does not appear to be as we have said, and he had previously been hopeful of their faith and compassionate towards them. In a hadith: "Some of them would strike him at times until he fell unconscious; when he recovered he would say: 'O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"

(Dayyaran): this is among the words of generality which are used in negation and similar contexts. Its pattern is fayyal, its root is diwar; the ya' and the waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so they were assimilated. It is said that from it comes dawwar, whose pattern is fa''al; both come from al-dawaran (circling), just as they say qiyam and qiwam, and the meaning is the meaning of ahad. From al-Suddi: one who dwells in a house. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is fayyal from al-dawr or from al-dar. End of quote. Al-dar is also from al-dawr, and its alif is converted from a waw.

﴿ولا يَلِدُوا إلّا فاجِرًا كَفّارًا﴾ ("and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers"): he described them, in the state of their begetting, by what they would come to of wickedness and disbelief. When he invoked against the disbelievers, he asked forgiveness for the believers, beginning with himself, then with those whose goodness was obligatory upon him, then for the believing men and women; so it is as though he and his parents were included among the believing men and believing women. The majority recited (wa-li-walidayya) ("and for my parents"), and it is apparent that the two of them are his father Lamak ibn Matushalakh and his mother Shamkha' bint Anush. It was also said: they are Adam and Hawwa'. Ibn Jubayr and al-Jahdari recited (wa-li-walidi) with a kasra on the dal, so either he specified his nearest father, or he meant all those who begot him back to Adam (peace be upon him). Ibn 'Abbas said: no father of Nuh (peace be upon him) between him and Adam (peace be upon him) disbelieved. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri and Zayd ibn 'Ali recited (wa-li-waladaya), the dual of walad, meaning Sam and Ham.

﴿ولِمَن دَخَلَ بَيْتِيَ﴾ ("and for whoever enters my house"): Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: my mosque. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: my law (shari'ati); he borrowed the word "house" for it, just as they say "the dome of Islam" and its "tent." It was also said: his ship. It was said: his dwelling.

﴿ولِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ والمُؤْمِناتِ﴾ ("and for the believing men and believing women"): he invoked for every believing man and woman in every nation. Al-tabar means destruction.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 71, verses 15–28 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: (p-340) ﴿Have you not seen how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon in them a light, and made the sun a lamp?﴾ ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth.﴾ ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a [definite] bringing forth.﴾ ﴿And God has made the earth for you a spread-out carpet.﴾ ﴿That you may travel therein along roads, wide ways.﴾ ﴿Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him not except in loss.﴾ ﴿And they have plotted a great plot.﴾ ﴿And they have said, 'Do not leave your gods, and do not leave Wadd or Suwa' or Yaghuth and Ya'uq and Nasr.'﴾ ﴿And they have already misled many. So increase not the wrongdoers except in error."﴾ ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter the Fire, and they found for themselves, besides God, no helpers.﴾ ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant.﴾ ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and not beget except wicked, ungrateful disbelievers.﴾ ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house believing and the believing men and believing women. And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction."﴾

When Noah, peace be upon him, alerted them to reflect upon themselves, and how they passed from one state to another, and the self is the nearest thing about which they reflect, he directed them to reflect upon the world, its upper and lower parts, and what God, exalted is He, placed in it. That is, in the upper world, of these two luminaries by which the existence of the universe is sustained. The explanation of (ṭibāqan, "in layers") has already been given in Surat al-Mulk. The pronoun in (fīhinna, "in them") refers to the heavens. It is said that the moon is in the lowest heaven. It is correct that the heavens be a container (ẓarf) for the moon, because it does not necessarily follow from a container that the contained fills it. You say, "Zayd is in the city," and he is in a part of it. The sun is not restricted to a container, so it is said: it is in the fourth, and it is said: in the fifth, and it is said: in winter it is in the fourth, and in summer in the seventh. This is something whose knowledge cannot be attained except from the science of astronomy (ʿilm al-hay'a). The people of this science mention that conclusive proofs stand for them confirming what they claim, and that in knowing that there is clear evidence of the greatness of God, His power, and the wondrous nature of His creation.

(Sirājan, "a lamp") by which the people of the world are illuminated, just as people are illuminated by a lamp in their houses. The moon did not reach the degree of the sun in brightness; therefore He said: "He who made the sun a radiance (ḍiyā') and the moon a light (nūr)," and ḍiyā' is stronger than nūr.

The (inbāt, "causing to grow") is a metaphor for creation. He created Adam from the earth, and his offspring came from him; therefore it is correct to attribute all of them to having been caused to grow from it. The accusative of (nabātan, "a growth") governed by (anbatakum, "caused you to grow") is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the extra element omitted, meaning a causing to grow; or it is by an implied verb, meaning: "so you grew a growth." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "He caused you to grow, so you grew," or it is in the accusative by (anbatakum) because it includes the meaning of (nabatum, "you grew"). End. I do not understand the meaning of this second opinion that he mentioned.

(Then He will return you into it) meaning: He will make you buried in it. (And bring you forth in a bringing forth) meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, and He emphasized it with the verbal noun, meaning: that is certainly going to happen.

(Carpet) you turn over upon it as a man turns over on his carpet. Its apparent meaning is that the earth is not spherical, but spread out. (Subulan, "roads") means ways; (fijājan, "wide") means broad. The discussion of (al-fajj, "wide path") has already passed in Surat (p-341) al-Ḥajj.

When they persisted in disobedience and treated him with the worst of words and deeds, (Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me"). The pronoun is for all of them. He had said to them: "And obey me," and he had remained among them the length God Most High specified: "a thousand years less fifty years" [al-ʿAnkabut: 14]. They had been given such abundance of provision that they would harvest twice in a month. (And followed) means: their common people and lowest, since it is not correct for the pronoun to return to all of them in the worship of idols.

(Whom wealth and children increase not) means: their leaders and great ones, those whose accumulated wealth and whose multitude of children were a cause of their loss in the Hereafter, and were the cause of their destruction in this world. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-A'raj, Mujahid, the two brothers (al-Akhawan, i.e., Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi', in the transmission of Kharija, read (wulduhu, "his children") with a ḍamma on the waw and sukūn on the lam. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan also, Abu Raja', Ibn Thabbat, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with fatḥa on both, and they are two dialects, like (bukhlun and bukhulun, "stinginess"). Al-Hasan also, al-Jahdari, Qatada, Zirr, Talha, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu ʿAmr, in one transmission, read it with kasra on the waw and sukūn on the lam. Abu Hatim said: it is possible that (al-wuld, with ḍamma) is the plural of (al-walad, "child"), like (khashab and khushub, "wood"). Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"O Bakr of Amina, blessed is her firstborn, of the sons of a chaste woman, with the fortunate Sa'd."

(And they plotted): it appears that it is conjoined to the relative clause of (man, "whom"), and the pronoun in (wa-makarū, "and they plotted") and (wa-qālū, "and they said") is plural by sense. Their plotting was their scheming in religion and inciting people against Noah, peace be upon him. The majority read (kubbāran, "great") with shadda on the bāʾ, and it is a form that has much intensification. ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar said: it is a Yemeni dialect, and upon it is the saying of the poet:

"A man is attached to the youths of generosity by the character of the noble, and not by beauty (wuḍḍāʾ)."

And the saying of another:

"A white woman who hunts hearts and captivates with beauty the heart of the Muslim reciter."

It is said: ḥussān, ṭuwwāl, and jummāl (intensive forms). ʿIsa, Ibn Muḥaysin and Abu al-Sammal read it with the bāʾ lightened, and it is an intensive form. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Ibn Muḥaysin, as narrated from him by Abu al-Ukhayrit Wahb ibn Wadih, read (kibbāran) with a kasra on the kāf and fatḥa on the bāʾ. Ibn al-Anbari said: it is a plural of (kabīr, "great"), as if he made "plotting" in place of "sins" or "deeds," and this is the end; he means that for this reason it was described with the plural.

(And they said), that is, their great ones to their followers; or they said, that is, all of them, some to others: (Do not abandon, "lā tadharunna" meaning: do not leave) (your gods), that is, your idols; this is general for all their idols, and then certain ones were specified after the chief idols, namely Wadd and what is conjoined to it. It is narrated that these were names of righteous men who lived in the early times. ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr said: they were children of Adam, and Wadd was the greatest of them and the most devoted to him. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and Muhammad ibn Qays said: they were sons of Adam and Noah, peace be upon them both; when they died, their forms were fashioned so as to remind people of their righteous deeds; then those who had fashioned them died, and others succeeded them who venerated them, and so on until they were worshipped. It was said: then those idols were transferred in their very forms. And it was said: rather only the names were transferred, to tribes of the Arabs. So Wadd belonged to Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal; Suwa' to Hudhayl, and it is said: to Hamdan; Yaghuth to Murad, and it is said: to Madhhij; Ya'uq to Hamdan, and it is said: to Murad; and Nasr to Himyar, and it is said: to Dhu al-Kala' of Himyar. For this reason the Arabs named people ʿAbd Wadd and ʿAbd Yaghuth. What occurred of this disagreement concerning Suwa', Yaghuth and Ya'uq may be that each of them had an idol named by this name, since it is far-fetched that the actual idols should survive; rather only the names remained, and they named their idols by them. Abu ʿUthman al-Nahdi said: I saw Yaghuth, and it was of lead, carried upon a bare-backed camel; they travelled with it and did not provoke it until it was the one that knelt, and when it knelt they dismounted and said: "It has approved the resting place for you," so they would dismount around it and pitch a structure for it. End. Al-Tha'labi said: Yaghuth belonged to Kahlan of Saba', passed down among them until it came to Hamdan, and in it Malik ibn Namat al-Hamdani says:

(p-342) "God makes feathers in the world and cuts them, but Yaghuth neither cuts nor makes feathers."

Al-Mawardi said: Wadd is the name of a worshipped idol; it was named Wadd because of their affection for it (widd). End. It was said: Wadd was in the form of a man, Suwa' in the form of a woman, Yaghuth in the form of a lion, Ya'uq in the form of a horse, and Nasr in the form of a vulture; and this contradicts what preceded, that they fashioned the forms of righteous people. Nafi', Abu Ja'far and Shayba, with a difference from them, read (wuddan) with ḍamma on the waw; al-Hasan, al-Aʿmash, Talha, and the rest of the seven read it with fatḥa. The poet said:

"May Wadd greet you, for we do not find it lawful for us the amusement of women, and the religion has decided."

Another said:

"So may Wadd greet you, from your love I met [her], and the gazelles upon the high ground of Tulala, sleeping."

It was said: he meant that idol. The majority read (wa-lā yaghūtha wa-yaʿūqa, "nor Yaghuth and Ya'uq") without tanwin. If they are Arabic, then their non-declension is due to definiteness and the form of the verb; if they are foreign, then due to foreignness and definiteness. Al-Ashhab read (yaghūthan wa-yaʿūqan) with tanwin on both. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: he made them a form (fa'ūl), and therefore he declined them. As for the common reading, they are two adjectives derived from (al-ghawth, "help") and (al-ʿawq, "hindrance") as verbs, and they are definite, so they are not declined, because two verbal features are combined: definiteness and resemblance to the imperfect verb. End. But this is confused. First, they cannot be a form (fa'ūl), because the root of yaghuththu is missing, and likewise ya'uqqu. Second, they are not adjectives derived from (al-ghawth) and (al-ʿawq), because (yafʿal) does not come as a noun or adjective; they were prevented from declension only for the reason we mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: al-Aʿmash read (wa-lā yaghūthan wa-yaʿūqan) with declension, and that is an error, because definiteness is binding and the verb pattern. End. But this is not an error; al-Aʿmash did not stand alone in this, rather al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli agreed with him. Its explanation is in one of two ways. The first: it came in the dialect of those who decline all that is not declined in the common Arabic usage, and this is a dialect, which al-Kisa'i and others narrated. The second: it was declined for the sake of matching what precedes and follows it of the indefinite, since before it is (wuddan wa-lā suwā'an, "Wadd nor Suwa'") and after it (wa-nasran, "and Nasr"), as they said regarding the declension of (salāsila, "chains") and (qawārīra qawārīra, "crystal, crystal") for whoever declines them for the sake of matching. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a problematic reading, because if they are Arabic or foreign there is non-declension in them; perhaps he intended the matching of endings, so he declined them because they correspond to their sisters which are declined: (wuddan wa-suwā'an wa-nasran), just as it was read (wa-ḍuḥāhā, "and its morning") with imāla because it occurs together with the imāla-forms for the sake of matching. End. Al-Zamakhshari did not realize that there is a dialect of some Arabs that declines everything that is not declined in the common usage, and therefore he found it problematic.

(And they have already misled) means: the leaders who are followed, (many): of their followers and common people. This is Noah, peace be upon him, informing about them of the misguidance that happened at their hands. Al-Hasan said: (and they have misled) means: the idols, the pronoun returning to them as it returns to rational beings, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "My Lord, they have indeed led astray many of the people" [Ibrahim: 36]; and it is made better by its return to the nearest mentioned referent, but its return to the leaders is more apparent, since they are the ones spoken of, and the meaning is more applicable to them. When he informed that they had gone astray much, he prayed against them for misguidance, saying: (And do not increase). It is conjoined to (and they have misled), since its implied sense is: "He said, and they have misled many"; so it is governed by the implied (said), whose quoted speech is (and they have misled). Harmony is not a condition in conjoining sentences; rather one may conjoin a sentence of command upon a sentence of information and the reverse, contrary to those who claim harmony is required. Al-Zamakhshari said, summarized: he conjoined (and do not increase) upon (My Lord, they have disobeyed me), meaning he said these two statements.

(Except in error). Al-Zamakhshari said: (If you say): how is it permissible that he should want error for them and call upon God to increase it? (I say): what is meant by error is that they be forsaken and deprived of divine favors, because of their obstinacy in disbelief and the despair of their belief; and that is good and beautiful, and it is permissible to supplicate with it, rather it would not be good to supplicate with the opposite. End. This is according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. He said: it is also possible that error means ruin and perdition, as He said: "And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction." Ibn Bahr said: (except in error) means: except in punishment, as in His saying: "Indeed, the criminals are in error and madness" [al-Qamar: 47]. It was said: except in loss. It was said: except in error concerning the affairs of their worldly life and the furthering of their plots and stratagems.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 71, verses 15–28 (part 2 of 2):

The majority of readers recited ﴿مِمّا خَطِيئاتِهِمْ﴾ (mimma khatee'atihim, "because of their sins") as a plural with the alif and ta', with hamza. Abu Raja' also recited it this way, except that he replaced the hamza with a ya' and assimilated the madd ya' into it. Al-Jahdari and Ubayd, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, recited it in the singular, with hamza. Al-Hasan, 'Isa and al-A'raj are reported to have recited it in more than one way. Abu 'Amr read khataya-hum as a broken plural (jam' taksir). This is a statement from Allah, Exalted, to the Messenger (ﷺ) that the supplication of Nuh (peace be upon him) has been answered. The ma here is extra, for emphasis (za'ida li-l-tawkid). As for (min), Ibn 'Atiyya said it indicates the starting point of the action (li-ibtida' al-ghaya), but it appears that it indicates causation (li-l-sabab).

'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited: min khatee'atihim ma ughriqu, with ma inserted between ughriqu and khatee'atihim. The majority recited (ughriqu) with hamza. Zayd ibn 'Ali recited ghurriqu with the shaddah. Both forms mean transitive causation (li-l-naql). Their sins (khatee'at) are shirk and what follows from it of the major sins. ﴿فَأُدْخِلُوا نارًا﴾ ("so they were made to enter a fire"): that is, Jahannam. The future is expressed in the past tense to indicate its certainty, and it is joined with fa' to indicate the intended sense of a ruling. Or the entry is used to express their being exposed to the Fire morning and evening, as He says: ﴿النّارُ يُعْرَضُونَ عَلَيْها﴾ ("The Fire, they are exposed to it," Ghafir: 46). Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or what is meant is the punishment of the grave." End of quote. Al-Dahhak said: they were drowned from one side and burned with fire from another side.

﴿فَلَمْ يَجِدُوا لَهم مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أنْصارًا﴾ ("and they did not find for themselves, besides Allah, any helpers"): an allusion to the absence of the power of their gods to help them. The supplication of Nuh (peace be upon him), after it had been revealed to him that ﴿لَنْ يُؤْمِنَ مِن قَوْمِكَ إلّا مَن قَدْ آمَنَ﴾ ("None of your people will believe except those who have already believed," Hud: 36), was said by Qatadah. Also from him: he did not invoke against them except after Allah had brought forth every believer from the loins, and had rendered the wombs of their women barren. This does not appear correct, because he said: ﴿إنَّكَ إنْ تَذَرْهم يُضِلُّوا عِبادَكَ﴾ ("If You leave them, they will mislead Your servants," and so on), and his saying ﴿ولا يَلِدُوا إلّا فاجِرًا كَفّارًا﴾ ("and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers") indicates that he had not rendered their wombs barren. Muhammad ibn Ka'b, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd also said this, but it does not appear to be as we have said, and he had previously been hopeful of their faith and compassionate towards them. In a hadith: "Some of them would strike him at times until he fell unconscious; when he recovered he would say: 'O Allah, forgive my people, for they do not know.'"

(Dayyaran): this is among the words of generality which are used in negation and similar contexts. Its pattern is fayyal, its root is diwar; the ya' and the waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so they were assimilated. It is said that from it comes dawwar, whose pattern is fa''al; both come from al-dawaran (circling), just as they say qiyam and qiwam, and the meaning is the meaning of ahad. From al-Suddi: one who dwells in a house. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is fayyal from al-dawr or from al-dar. End of quote. Al-dar is also from al-dawr, and its alif is converted from a waw.

﴿ولا يَلِدُوا إلّا فاجِرًا كَفّارًا﴾ ("and they will beget none but wicked disbelievers"): he described them, in the state of their begetting, by what they would come to of wickedness and disbelief. When he invoked against the disbelievers, he asked forgiveness for the believers, beginning with himself, then with those whose goodness was obligatory upon him, then for the believing men and women; so it is as though he and his parents were included among the believing men and believing women. The majority recited (wa-li-walidayya) ("and for my parents"), and it is apparent that the two of them are his father Lamak ibn Matushalakh and his mother Shamkha' bint Anush. It was also said: they are Adam and Hawwa'. Ibn Jubayr and al-Jahdari recited (wa-li-walidi) with a kasra on the dal, so either he specified his nearest father, or he meant all those who begot him back to Adam (peace be upon him). Ibn 'Abbas said: no father of Nuh (peace be upon him) between him and Adam (peace be upon him) disbelieved. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri and Zayd ibn 'Ali recited (wa-li-waladaya), the dual of walad, meaning Sam and Ham.

﴿ولِمَن دَخَلَ بَيْتِيَ﴾ ("and for whoever enters my house"): Ibn 'Abbas and the majority said: my mosque. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: my law (shari'ati); he borrowed the word "house" for it, just as they say "the dome of Islam" and its "tent." It was also said: his ship. It was said: his dwelling.

﴿ولِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ والمُؤْمِناتِ﴾ ("and for the believing men and believing women"): he invoked for every believing man and woman in every nation. Al-tabar means destruction.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 71, verses 15–28 (part 1 of 2):**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: (p-340) ﴿Have you not seen how God created seven heavens in layers?﴾ ﴿And made the moon in them a light, and made the sun a lamp?﴾ ﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth.﴾ ﴿Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in a [definite] bringing forth.﴾ ﴿And God has made the earth for you a spread-out carpet.﴾ ﴿That you may travel therein along roads, wide ways.﴾ ﴿Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me and followed one whose wealth and children increase him not except in loss.﴾ ﴿And they have plotted a great plot.﴾ ﴿And they have said, 'Do not leave your gods, and do not leave Wadd or Suwa' or Yaghuth and Ya'uq and Nasr.'﴾ ﴿And they have already misled many. So increase not the wrongdoers except in error."﴾ ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned and then made to enter the Fire, and they found for themselves, besides God, no helpers.﴾ ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant.﴾ ﴿Indeed, if You leave them, they will mislead Your servants and not beget except wicked, ungrateful disbelievers.﴾ ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house believing and the believing men and believing women. And do not increase the wrongdoers except in destruction."﴾

When Noah, peace be upon him, alerted them to reflect upon themselves, and how they passed from one state to another, and the self is the nearest thing about which they reflect, he directed them to reflect upon the world, its upper and lower parts, and what God, exalted is He, placed in it. That is, in the upper world, of these two luminaries by which the existence of the universe is sustained. The explanation of (ṭibāqan, "in layers") has already been given in Surat al-Mulk. The pronoun in (fīhinna, "in them") refers to the heavens. It is said that the moon is in the lowest heaven. It is correct that the heavens be a container (ẓarf) for the moon, because it does not necessarily follow from a container that the contained fills it. You say, "Zayd is in the city," and he is in a part of it. The sun is not restricted to a container, so it is said: it is in the fourth, and it is said: in the fifth, and it is said: in winter it is in the fourth, and in summer in the seventh. This is something whose knowledge cannot be attained except from the science of astronomy (ʿilm al-hay'a). The people of this science mention that conclusive proofs stand for them confirming what they claim, and that in knowing that there is clear evidence of the greatness of God, His power, and the wondrous nature of His creation.

(Sirājan, "a lamp") by which the people of the world are illuminated, just as people are illuminated by a lamp in their houses. The moon did not reach the degree of the sun in brightness; therefore He said: "He who made the sun a radiance (ḍiyā') and the moon a light (nūr)," and ḍiyā' is stronger than nūr.

The (inbāt, "causing to grow") is a metaphor for creation. He created Adam from the earth, and his offspring came from him; therefore it is correct to attribute all of them to having been caused to grow from it. The accusative of (nabātan, "a growth") governed by (anbatakum, "caused you to grow") is a verbal noun (maṣdar) with the extra element omitted, meaning a causing to grow; or it is by an implied verb, meaning: "so you grew a growth." Al-Zamakhshari said: the meaning is "He caused you to grow, so you grew," or it is in the accusative by (anbatakum) because it includes the meaning of (nabatum, "you grew"). End. I do not understand the meaning of this second opinion that he mentioned.

(Then He will return you into it) meaning: He will make you buried in it. (And bring you forth in a bringing forth) meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, and He emphasized it with the verbal noun, meaning: that is certainly going to happen.

(Carpet) you turn over upon it as a man turns over on his carpet. Its apparent meaning is that the earth is not spherical, but spread out. (Subulan, "roads") means ways; (fijājan, "wide") means broad. The discussion of (al-fajj, "wide path") has already passed in Surat (p-341) al-Ḥajj.

When they persisted in disobedience and treated him with the worst of words and deeds, (Noah said, "My Lord, they have disobeyed me"). The pronoun is for all of them. He had said to them: "And obey me," and he had remained among them the length God Most High specified: "a thousand years less fifty years" [al-ʿAnkabut: 14]. They had been given such abundance of provision that they would harvest twice in a month. (And followed) means: their common people and lowest, since it is not correct for the pronoun to return to all of them in the worship of idols.

(Whom wealth and children increase not) means: their leaders and great ones, those whose accumulated wealth and whose multitude of children were a cause of their loss in the Hereafter, and were the cause of their destruction in this world. Ibn al-Zubayr, al-Hasan, al-Nakha'i, al-A'raj, Mujahid, the two brothers (al-Akhawan, i.e., Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi', in the transmission of Kharija, read (wulduhu, "his children") with a ḍamma on the waw and sukūn on the lam. Al-Sulami and al-Hasan also, Abu Raja', Ibn Thabbat, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Nafi', ʿAsim and Ibn ʿAmir read it with fatḥa on both, and they are two dialects, like (bukhlun and bukhulun, "stinginess"). Their plotting was their scheming in religion and inciting people against Noah, peace be upon him. "A man is attached to the youths of generosity by the character of the noble, and not by beauty (wuḍḍāʾ)."

And the saying of another:

"A white woman who hunts hearts and captivates with beauty the heart of the Muslim reciter."

(And they said), that is, their great ones to their followers; or they said, that is, all of them, some to others: (Do not abandon, "lā tadharunna" meaning: do not leave) (your gods), that is, your idols; this is general for all their idols, and then certain ones were specified after the chief idols, namely Wadd and what is conjoined to it. End. Al-Tha'labi said: Yaghuth belonged to Kahlan of Saba', passed down among them until it came to Hamdan, and in it Malik ibn Namat al-Hamdani says:
